source.title: Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders
source.authors: Leo Gao; Tom Dupré la Tour; Henk Tillman; Gabriel Goh; Rajan Troll; A. Radford; I. Sutskever; Jan Leike; Jeffrey Wu

page_placements.theme: Optimisation and data-statistics artifact latents (dense, unigram, position-locked)

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies SAE scaling and feature quality, but does not test whether features split across dictionary sizes, whether child features partition parent inputs, or the proposed challenges to that pattern.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scaling, reconstruction, probe, explanation, and ablation results, but these do not measure feature splitting across dictionary sizes. Its latent clustering and recurring-feature observations are related to SAE feature geometry or identity, but do not test the specified versions. Results from cited work are not included.
record.test_reason: The paper studies TopK SAE scaling laws, reconstruction, probe, explanation and ablation-sparsity metrics across dictionary sizes. It never matches features across dictionary sizes, checks whether finer latents cover a coarser latent's inputs, studies parent/child firing or absorption, or decomposes larger-SAE latents into smaller ones. Its qualitative recurring-dense-feature and subspace observations concern latent identity and geometry, not splitting.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that TopK SAEs give clean scaling laws in n and k with few dead latents, and that their feature-quality metrics generally improve with dictionary size. The effect of k is mixed, and the trends break as k nears d_model. They say nothing about feature splitting.
record.recipe_differences: Uses TopK sparse autoencoders and evaluates scaling and feature-quality metrics; it does not apply a feature-splitting or cross-dictionary matching procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with dictionary size, active-latent count, and layer for the paper's scaling and quality metrics; these are not measurements of the claim's feature-splitting pattern.

fits_no_version.finding: The densest GPT-2 small layer 8 latents (position, first-token and repetition features) recur across SAEs trained differently, including with different n. They often have opposing latents with decoder cosine near -1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dense, uninterpretable latents recur stably across SAE sizes, possibly as optimisation artifacts.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE encoder directions fall into two fuzzy subspaces: about 25% of latents use about 25% of dimensions and activate on few vocabulary tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents cluster into residual-stream subspaces that differ in token diversity.

record.problems: The observations closest to feature identity or geometry are qualitative or described as fuzzy, and the paper does not match features across dictionaries or test whether inputs are partitioned.
record.rows_left_out: Scaling laws, reconstruction loss, probes, explanation scores, and ablation-sparsity results are omitted because they do not measure feature splitting or the related latent identity and geometry findings recorded here.

untested.parts: Replacement of coarse features by finer ones as n grows, input coverage, directional proximity
Splitting in GPT-4-scale models or in open SAE releases (TopK SAEs were released but not analysed for splitting)
Nested feature families mirroring a concept hierarchy
Absorption, i.e. a parent latent failing to fire where a child latent takes over, and its robustness to size or sparsity
Decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents; novel latents
Whether the training objective causes splitting; Matryoshka objectives (the Multi-TopK objective targets progressive codes, not splitting)

record.verdict_notes: The paper is not an original source for this claim. Nearby but unrelated observations: modal latent density falls as n grows, and the authors note that explanation failures worsen as features get sparser and more specific. Neither measures splitting.

versions.untested_parts: Feature replacement across dictionary sizes, input coverage by child features, and directional proximity.
Splitting at scale or across open SAE releases.
Nested split-feature families, their proximity, and whether they mirror a conceptual hierarchy.
Parent-child firing overlap and whether changing SAE size or sparsity fixes absorption.
Decomposition of larger latents into smaller latents and the appearance of novel latents.
Whether splitting is caused by the SAE objective on hierarchical inputs or changed by Matryoshka SAEs.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Manually compared the densest latents across autoencoders trained in different ways, including with different dictionary sizes.

conditions.value: various layer 8 autoencoders; exact sizes not stated

rows.measure: Recurring latent feature identities among the densest latents
rows.value: The two densest latents were always the same two position-related features; the third densest was a first-token-position feature; a repetition feature also recurred.
rows.note: This is a qualitative observation across autoencoders, not a test of feature splitting, matching child features, or input partitioning.
rows.check: Qualitative note that the densest latents recur across GPT-2 small layer 8 SAEs of varying size. It concerns stability of dense features, not coarse features splitting into finer ones. Exact SAE sizes are not stated. Linking to none is correct.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix E.6, Recurring dense features in GPT-2 small

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed encoder directions using SVD, then ordered latent projections using pairwise distances and a one-dimensional UMAP embedding.

conditions.value: latent encoder directions; SAE size not stated

rows.measure: Grouping of latent projections into subspaces
rows.value: The authors describe two fuzzily separated subspaces: about 25% of latents project mostly onto about 25% of dimensions, while the remaining 75% project mostly onto the remaining 75%.
rows.note: This measures subspace structure within an SAE, not geometrically close families of split features across dictionaries or a hierarchy of concepts.
rows.check: Subspace clustering of encoder directions within a single SAE (size not stated; the figure suggests about 32k latents). No cross-size comparison and no concept hierarchy, so it does not bear on V3. Linking to none is correct.

relation.reason: The paper cites Bricken et al. 2023. It notes in passing that features get sparser and more specific as SAEs scale (Sec 4.3), but does not test this. 'discusses' fits; 'cites_only' would also be defensible.

tranche.reason: The paper never mentions feature splitting or absorption, and never matches features across dictionary sizes. E.6 is about dense features that recur across SAEs, not about coarse features splitting into finer ones.

source_check.notes: The E.6 observation is qualitative and gives no exact SAE sizes. Sec 4.3 says in passing that features get 'sparser and more specific' as SAEs scale, without testing it. The pack lists 1 of 2 record rows; the other row was not given, so it was not checked.

statements.correction: Text (E.6): the authors manually examined the densest latents across GPT-2 small layer 8 autoencoders trained in different ways, e.g. with different numbers of total latents. The two densest are always the same position features (~40% and ~35% active). The third is always a first-token-position feature (~30%). A recurring repetition feature is ~20% dense. Opposing latents with decoder cosine near -1 often appear among the top ten densest. The first-token and repetition latents seem to always have one.
